messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan, a 38-year-old high school teacher, had always prided himself on his ability to create a safe and welcoming classroom environment. However, after a traumatic mugging three months ago, his world had become a place of constant anxiety and fear. The incident had occurred one evening while he was walking home from his favorite coffee shop. A group of men had approached him, demanding his wallet. He could still taste the bitterness of the coffee he had just sipped, a sensory detail that would return unbidden whenever memories of that night surfaced, flooding his mind with the visceral reality of his terror. These memories would pull him back to that night, making every unexpected sound or crowded space feel like a direct threat, as if the danger was still lurking just beneath the surface. Each time that memory resurfaced, it would trigger a fresh wave of panic, leaving him hyper-aware of his surroundings and convinced that danger was lurking just around the corner. Those moments replayed relentlessly, forcing their way into his thoughts at the most inconvenient times, making it impossible for him to focus on anything else. Since the mugging, Ethan had developed a keen sensitivity to crowded places. He avoided the bustling hallways at school and steered clear of busy shopping malls, acutely aware of how overwhelming the throngs of people could be. The anxiety would grip him, and he would find himself scanning the room for exits, a habit that had taken hold the moment he stepped out of his house that night. Each time he felt that tightness in his chest, memories of the mugging rushed back with vivid clarity, making him relive the moment and reinforcing the belief that he was always in danger. Each instance of anxiety would trigger thoughts like “this is what my life is now — always on edge,” solidifying his negative belief that the world was not just unsafe, but hostile and untrustworthy. The vivid memories of the mugging made him feel as if danger lurked behind every unfamiliar face. As those memories flooded back, they reinforced his belief that he could trust no one and that every encounter was a potential threat to his safety. Every time he encountered those reminders, it solidified his belief that the world was an untrustworthy place, one where he was perpetually at risk. Each time he was reminded of that night, whether through a crowded hallway or an unexpected sound, the sensation of threat intensified, reinforcing his belief that he was never truly safe. He had come to believe that he could trust no one, a notion that was reinforced each time he felt the weight of a stranger's gaze upon him; he would scrutinize their expressions, searching for any hint of threat. This constant vigilance transformed the world into a perilous place, one where he could no longer feel safe even in familiar surroundings. Ethan’s struggles with loud noises had also intensified. The sudden sounds would trigger his memories of the chaos during the mugging, making him acutely aware of how vulnerable he felt, and reinforcing his conviction that the world outside was filled with peril. Sounds that once seemed mundane now sent him spiraling into panic. The clatter of chairs in the staff room would send his heart racing, reminiscent of the chaos that had ensued during the robbery. Each unexpected noise triggered a cascade of memories, making him feel as though he was reliving the event, amplifying the threat he felt from his surroundings. This relentless cycle of recollection not only heightened his anxiety but also solidified his conviction that he was weak for letting this happen to him, deepening his negative self-image. These memories not only deepened his fear but also made him question his own worth, leading him to believe that he had somehow failed to protect himself from harm. Each time the flashback surged to the forefront, it echoed the belief that he was weak for allowing the mugging to happen, reinforcing a negative self-image that he could not shake off. Every time a flashback surfaced, he was left grappling with the thought that he was not just a victim, but someone who had let this happen, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy. The world had become a cacophony of potential dangers, each sound a reminder of the injustice he felt — that someone had violated his sense of security and that nothing had been done to hold the perpetrators accountable. These memories, steeped in the violence of that night, deepened his conviction that he was powerless, feeding into a belief that he was now marked by his trauma. This belief only deepened his sense of helplessness, making it harder for him to shake off the memories that haunted him. Ethan's internal narrative had shifted dramatically since the mugging. He frequently ruminated on how the institutions that were supposed to protect him had failed. He could not shake the feeling that the police had been dismissive when he reported the incident, viewing him as just another victim in a city filled with crime. This sense of injustice only deepened with every flashback he experienced, further entrenching his belief that he was a target in an uncaring world, making him feel even more powerless. In the midst of these memories, the ever-present threat whispered to him that he was not just a victim of circumstance, but someone destined to be fearful and small in a world that had shown him its worst. This perception of institutional failure compounded his sense of injustice, further entrenching him in the belief that the world was an inherently dangerous place. With the weight of that injustice pressing down on him, he felt an ever-present threat, as if the world was conspiring against him, confirming his fears that he was always unsafe. This constant sense of threat fed into his belief that he was forever marked by his trauma, making him feel even more powerless and trapped in a cycle of fear. Each time he recalled the robbery, he felt a surge of anger and betrayal that only served to reinforce his negative appraisals of his environment and the people within it. In his classroom, Ethan tried to maintain a façade of normalcy, but his students could sense the change in him. He found himself avoiding driving with colleagues after school, as the thought of being in a confined space with others made him uneasy. The fear of being trapped felt all too real, a reflection of his ongoing battle with the trauma that loomed over him. This constant sense of threat made him believe that he was no longer capable of navigating even the simplest situations, reinforcing his negative self-appraisal and convincing him that he was forever burdened by his past. This chronic sense of threat whispered to him that he was no longer in control, reinforcing his negative self-perception and convincing him that he was forever marked by the trauma he endured. He had become increasingly isolated, withdrawing from social gatherings and even avoiding family outings, fearful that the memories would intrude and disrupt moments that should be joyful. Every time he felt that familiar surge of anxiety, it confirmed his belief that he was a burden to those around him, reinforcing his reluctance to engage with others, further deepening his isolation. The constant sense of threat that accompanied his isolation only reinforced his belief that he was a burden to those around him, further deepening his reluctance to engage with others. Now, sitting in the therapist’s office, Ethan felt both a sense of relief and apprehension. He had finally sought help, driven by the overwhelming weight of his distress and the realization that he could no longer navigate this tumultuous sea of emotions alone. What frightened him most was the thought of remaining in this cycle of fear and avoidance, paralyzed by the belief that the world was dangerous and that he could never truly feel safe again. This ongoing sense of threat had led him to conclude that he was no longer the person he once was, someone who could engage with the world without fear, reinforcing the notion that he was now trapped in a life that felt entirely unmanageable. This ongoing threat loomed large in his mind, whispering to him that he was no longer the person he once was — someone who could trust the world and feel secure. The vivid recollection of the mugging left Ethan feeling vulnerable and exposed, as if the threat was not just a past event but an ever-present reality, stalking him in his daily life. Yet, deep down, he hoped to reclaim his life, to find a way to break free from the grip of his memories and allow himself to heal. Recognizing how easily triggers could pull him back into the memories of that night made him feel even more disconnected from those he loved, further solidifying his belief that he was a burden. The intrusive thoughts and memories that surfaced left him convinced that he would never be able to fully participate in life again, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy and despair. Each time he felt that familiar surge of anxiety, he was reminded of the trauma that had altered his life so drastically, reinforcing the notion that he was not just a victim but someone forever changed by fear. The accumulation of these memories and feelings made him see himself as a burden to those he loved, deepening his belief that he was unworthy of their support and love. Each time memories of the mugging surfaced, they brought with them the conviction that he was now living in a world where he could never truly feel secure, deepening his sense of being marked by trauma.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not establish that triggers influence or lead to the formation of memories.
The vignette does not establish that triggers influence or lead to negative appraisals.
The vignette does not establish that negative appraisals influence or lead to the formation of memories.
The vignette does not establish that memories influence or create a sense of threat.
The vignette does not establish that memories influence or lead to negative appraisals.
The vignette does not establish that memories influence or lead to triggers.
The vignette does not establish that a sense of threat influences or leads to negative appraisals.
The vignette does not establish that a sense of threat influences or leads to triggers.
